messages.content: Write a post about what a software company learned from a year of remote work. Around 250 words.

output:
A year ago we sent everyone home and told them to figure it out. Here's what actually held up.

Meetings got worse before they got better. We spent the first few months trying to replicate the office in Zoom form — standups, all-hands, the whole calendar — and it wore people out. What worked was cutting meetings by roughly a third and writing more instead. Decisions that used to get made verbally in a hallway now live in a doc, which turned out to be an upgrade: you can search a doc six months later, you can't search a hallway.

Timezones stopped being a hiring constraint and became a design constraint. Once a third of the team wasn't online at 10am, synchronous became the exception, not the default. Engineers went weeks without a live conversation with their manager and shipped fine, because the code review and the ticket carried the context that used to live in someone's head.

The surprise was onboarding. New hires who joined remote ramped up slower for the first month, then caught up and often overtook people who'd started in the office — because everything they needed to learn was written down for them, instead of absorbed by osmosis from sitting near the right person.

What we didn't solve: casual collision. The random conversation that turns into a feature idea doesn't happen over Slack, and we haven't found a real substitute. A few teams tried scheduled "coffee chats" and mostly hated them.

Net result: less time in meetings, better documentation, and a hiring pool that's no longer bounded by a 45-minute commute.
